Hi, we're team CivicOps. In Mumbai, when you complain about a flooded road you never learn who owns it, when it's due, or if it was really fixed. And nobody can follow the money. We built one app that fixes both, and adds a QR code to every road.

Three things nobody in Mumbai can see today. Who owns my complaint. Where the money went. And when a road's free-repair guarantee ends. In the organisers' dataset alone, 13 crore rupees were billed in one monsoon, and almost 500 repair bills were paid while the road was still under the contractor's guarantee.

Our answer is one trail for each. A complaint goes from report to the right ward, a visible deadline, photo proof, and a person's verification. A rupee goes from budget to work order to bill to evidence to review. And a road: scan the QR, see the guarantee, the spend, and report a defect that should be fixed free.

A resident reports in a few taps: category, two or three questions, GPS or a pin on the real Mumbai map. Before submitting they already see the ward, the team and the urgency. Juhu goes to K West; a bare 'Andheri' asks which one. Red means first action in 5 hours. Missed deadlines escalate automatically. The officer and the contractor are named and alerted.

On the ticket page, everything is on one screen: who owns it, who is doing the work, the next step, the deadline, and a progress trail with the time of every step. When the work is done, the reviewer compares before and after photos with a slider. Claude describes what changed and what it cannot verify. A person always makes the call and records why.

Now the money, for anyone, no login. For each of the 24 wards we follow the money from the approved budget to the work order, the bill, the evidence and the review. Four wards billed more than their budget. 3.43 crore is questioned, and each work order is counted once, so nothing is double counted.

One real example from the data. A repair on Link Road in Juhu, work order 1590. Billed 23,311 rupees. The city's own rate card says 12,220. That is 11,091 rupees, or 91 percent, above. And it broke again within 30 days. We never call it fraud. Anyone can ask a question; the ward office must answer by a deadline; if it doesn't, it escalates in public; an independent reviewer decides.

Fairness matters as much as accuracy. Contractors are compared only with what is normal for the repair method they used, and delays on heavy rain days are taken out. Normal variation is never flagged; a bill must be beyond 1.3 times the rate card. Every flag shows its maths and source rows. And for budget smarts, each ward gets a next-rupee plan that ranks roads by risk and recommends repairs that last.

Our newest idea: a QR on every road. Every repair has a defect liability period: concrete 10 years, mastic 5, asphalt 3. Inside it, defects are the contractor's job, free. Scan the board and you see the guarantee counting down, who must fix it, every rupee spent, and a red 'paid twice?' flag when the city paid for repairs during the guarantee. One tap reports a defect on that exact road. Scan the code on the right to try it.

For the ward office and the commissioner, the live dashboard: the whole city on a real map of Mumbai, all 24 wards, urgent tickets, deadline health and a live feed of every action, refreshing every ten seconds. It's what we put on the big screen.

This is not a mock-up. It is live on Vercel with a Postgres database. Five roles, each seeing only what it should, enforced in the database. 57 automated tests and 11 end-to-end browser scenarios, all passing on the live demo. Every page in English, Marathi and Hindi. All 17 files of the organisers' dataset are used.

Against your five criteria: audit accuracy, every flag shows its maths. Fair accountability, rain and method adjustments plus a response window and independent review. Budget smarts, the next-rupee plan. Connects the trail, complaint to work order to bill to question to decision. And usable: phone first, three languages, live right now.

What's next: a 90-day pilot in one ward with real completion certificates and guarantee clauses, QR boards on the first 50 roads, and WhatsApp alerts before a guarantee ends. Then all 24 wards, tender import, and open data.
Every complaint has an owner. Every rupee has a reason. Every road carries its own QR. Scan the code and try it with one-click demo accounts. Thank you.
